searches.note: Twenty eight searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's. Ten were restricted to a house's own domain (tiopepe.com and gonzalezbyass.com twice, lagitana.es once, grupoestevez.com twice, lustau.es three times, harveyssherry.com and harveys.es twice) and two to the Consejo Regulador's sherry.wine, and are read as primary through their summaries; one more to five merchants' and the tourist board's domains, and the rest went to the open web for second sources (the founders, the dates of 1844, 1890 and 1964, Pastrana, the criaderas and yeasts of Inocente, Lustau's history and San Emilio's grapes, Harveys of 1796, 1822, 1882 and the 1970s). The shared search is the Consejo's serving temperatures, used by all five. No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; no fact that rests on no source was kept.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the houses' own pages for their own dates, vineyards and methods, then to the open web for the second source of each date and person, then to the Consejo Regulador for the styles and the serve.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail was found in one account only, or the accounts disagreed, it was cut or said with less (1890, the newcomer, the fifty year old vines of Pastrana, the Ponche liqueur, the Medium Dry Amontillado, the first Fino of Jerez abroad, the first merchant in blue glass).
Claims of a first that rest on the house alone were taken out of the stories; claims of the house's own dates and vineyards stand, hedged as the house's account where they are its telling.

Sources whose title or address names a living person, or that are a writer's own site (Sherry Notes, a Master of Wine's site, Jancis Robinson's articles), were met in the results but never cited in the fragment or here; the fragment's own sources were left as the author wrote them, and the new ones are listed per record under extraSources.

tested: Founded 1835 by a young man of twenty three: the house's story, Selectus Wines (born 1812, the year of the constitution called La Pepa) and Spanish Wine Lover agree on 1835 and the age; confirmed. The founder stays described, as the author chose: his death in 1887 is in one account only.

The uncle José, Tío Pepe, who taught him the craft: the house's own story page says the uncle taught him all the secrets of the art of making wine in Jerez; confirmed. His surname still differs between the house's pages (Ángel y Vargas, Ángel de la Peña), so the record names him only José, as it does.

1844, casks to England, the agent who became a partner and gave the name Byass: the house's news page and Master of Malt give the first casks of Tío Pepe to the United Kingdom in 1844 and the English agent; several accounts date his partnership to 1855. Confirmed. The house's claim to be the first sherry winery to export the Fino style is its own alone, so the story now says its first casks of this Fino abroad.

1935, the centenary: the house's news page says its head of advertising, who took the post in 1934, created the figure in 1935 with guitar, hat and jacket; the lit sign over the Puerta del Sol later (the house gives 1958 in one page, other accounts 1935 or 1936). The story's later stands; confirmed.

The making: Palomino Fino alone, at least four years under flor in American oak by solera (the house's product page, a merchant's sheet), 15 per cent (the Consejo's Fino page, merchants); confirmed. Fortified to 15 per cent is the Consejo's figure for Fino.

The sites, Macharnudo and Carrascal: the house's Una Palma page, its En Rama 2016 page (single estate vineyards Macharnudo and Carrascal on pure albariza) and its night harvest page (La Racha in Macharnudo, for the founding solera of Tío Pepe); confirmed.
Una Palma: the house's page gives a few selected casks of the Tío Pepe solera and more than six years under flor; the record said at least six: changed.
The serve, 6 to 8 degrees Celsius in a bucket of ice and water: the Consejo's serving page gives exactly this; confirmed.

The questions: one key each; the distractors of the first are four reasons, the second four places; the explanation of the first rests on the Codex's region record (seventeen per cent kills the flor). Sound.
The rules: nobody living named; no price, no score; the line on the Fino a guest is most likely to know was a rank of fame and is changed; British; no dash. Sound after the change.

changed.why: A first for all of Jerez is the house's own claim and nobody else's; the house's first shipment of Tío Pepe in 1844 is in its pages and two merchants' accounts.

tested: Founded 1792 (the library's year): the house's home page, Selectus Wines and Spanish Wine Lover; confirmed. The founder bought a small storage bodega in the lower town by the river from his father in law, by Selectus and the house; one account instead has a José Antonio Hidalgo arrive early in the eighteenth century and his son found the bodega, so the founder is no longer called a newcomer.

The name La Gitana and the Málaga legend: Selectus dates the brand to around 1890; a second account puts the gypsy woman's bar in Málaga at the end of the nineteenth century; Glengarry Wines tells of a bar in Málaga run by a gypsy; Spanish Wine Lover says the house kept the name and drew a gypsy woman on the label when it began to bottle early in the twentieth century; the label painted about 1900 by the father of the composer Joaquín Turina. 1890 is in one account only, so the story now says late in the nineteenth century, the story goes. A family business study of UIC dates the first record of the brand to an invoice of 1904; reported, not used.
The vineyards: the house's own page gives La Gitana's grapes from the El Cuadrado estate in the Balbaina Alta pago and calls Miraflores a purely Atlantic pago; the sites line now says so.

The making: the house's page says the wines enter soleras dating from 1792 and spend three years at its San Fermín bodega in the lower town, open to the river; confirmed (the record says about three years and the bodegas by the river).
Pastrana: Bodeboca and Vinissimus put the Pastrana vineyard in the Miraflores pago on albariza; the vines' age of fifty years is in Vinissimus alone: cut from others and story.

1964, added: the ministry's bulletin of April 1964, Alimarket's half century of the appellation and the Universidad Pablo de Olavide give 1964 for the separate appellation Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda, under the one Consejo Regulador; added to keep two dated turning points once 1890 left.
The serve, 6 to 8 degrees Celsius: the Consejo's serving page; confirmed.

The questions: the wine question has one key and four reasons; the story question's places are four of one kind and the bar in Málaga is in three accounts. Sound; the explanation no longer dates the name.
The rules: nobody living named; no rank (one merchant calls La Gitana the best selling Manzanilla in the world, which the record rightly leaves out); British; no dash. Sound.

changed.was: around 1890 the family gave its Manzanilla the name La Gitana. The story goes that a gypsy woman sold the house's wine at her bar in Málaga, and that her customers asked for it as the gypsy's wine; a portrait of a gypsy woman, painted for the firm, became its label.
changed.now: late in that century, the story goes, a gypsy woman sold the house's Manzanilla, not yet branded, at her bar in Málaga, and her customers asked for it as the gypsy's wine. The family kept the name La Gitana, and a portrait of a gypsy woman, painted for the firm, became its label.
changed.why: 1890 is in one account only; the end of the nineteenth century is in two, and the bar in Málaga in three.

tested: founded empty (the library leaves it empty): the house's pages give the legend of 1264 and trade records of 1430, Wikipedia gives 1430, and the house's group says the company was formed in 1875 (another account 1837). Empty is the true answer; kept.

1264: the house's own pages tell that one of the 24 knights who fought with Alfonso X to take Jerez was a Valdespino, whom the king rewarded with a vineyard; the record said land granted to the knights, who began to make wine: changed to the house's telling, hedged as the story goes.
1430, 1883: the house's group and Wikipedia give the records of 1430; Wikipedia and a second account give the royal household's supplier from 1883; confirmed.

1999: Wikipedia and the house's group give the Estévez group from 1999; the house's own word is that it joined the group, so the story now says the house passed to it rather than that the family sold it.

Inocente: the house's sheet gives the grapes only from the Viña Valdespino in Macharnudo Alto, fermentation in American oak butts, a solera and ten criaderas, nine to ten months as sobretabla, and an average of ten years (its news, about eleven years under flor); confirmed. Native yeasts that settle in the butts, and ten criaderas where others use three or four, in two merchants' and press accounts (Skurnik, Directo al Paladar); the grapes' own yeasts became native yeasts, and far more became more.
The serve, 6 to 8 degrees Celsius: the Consejo's serving page; confirmed.

The questions: the wine question's four wines are of one kind and only Inocente is a single vineyard Fino fermented in cask; the story question's four years are the house's four dates. Sound after the wording of the reward.
The rules: nobody living named; no price; the line on the single vineyard Fino an examiner asks for follows the library and ranks nothing; British; no dash. Sound.

tested: Founded 1896 (the library's year), the court clerk, the estate Nuestra Señora de la Esperanza, vines and wine in his spare time sold to the large houses: the house's From Jerez to the world page, Wikipedia, Skurnik and a Jerez blog; confirmed.

1931: the house and Wikipedia give the daughter's purchase of a bodega near the centre of Jerez and the move of the soleras; confirmed. The husband's move to the Santiago quarter in the 1940s, by the house; undated in the record, rightly, since 1940 and the 1940s are given.

1945, own brands (Papirusa, Jarana, Escuadrilla, Emperatriz Eugenia, Cinta de Oro): the house's About page; 1981, the first Almacenista bottlings: the house's About and Almacenistas pages; 1990, merged with the Luis Caballero group, a family wine and spirits company: the house's About page and Wikipedia (acquired by Grupo Caballero). Confirmed; the Ponche Caballero liqueur was in no source read and is cut.

San Emilio: the house's page and its sheet give 100 per cent Pedro Ximénez, the grapes laid in the sun until almost raisins, a slow fermentation halted to keep the sugar, and twelve years in contact with air in Jerez; the Consejo's Pedro Ximénez page gives the asoleo, fortification with wine spirit to stop the fermentation and oxidative ageing only; confirmed.

Solera Familiar, earlier sold as Solera Reserva: Berry Bros. and Rudd's address carries solera reserva beside a Solera Familiar title, and Grape Expectations sells it as Solera Reserva; kept as the author wrote it.
East India Solera: the house's own page makes it a cream of Oloroso and Pedro Ximénez that recalls casks warmed in the holds of ships bound for the East Indies; the note now says so.
The serve, 12 to 14 degrees Celsius: the Consejo's serving page gives 12 to 14 for Pedro Ximénez; confirmed.
VOS twenty and VORS thirty in the trap: the library and the house's own VORS and SC sheets (thirty and twenty); confirmed.
The questions: four ways to sweeten, one right; four years of the house's story, each placed in the explanation. Sound.

The rules: nobody living named (the founder, his daughter and her husband are described; the 1990 partner is a company); no price; no rank (the house's page on being the most awarded Spanish winery at a competition was read and left out), and the story's clearest way to teach became a clear way; British; no dash. Sound after the change.

A search for the grapes' origin found a merchant placing Lustau's Single Cask Pedro Ximénez grapes in Montilla-Moriles and the house's own blog saying the grape grows in both Montilla-Moriles and Jerez; nothing names San Emilio's source.

tested: Founded 1796 in Denmark Street (the plan's year; the house is not in the library): Wikipedia, the Science Museum Group (William Perry trading from 12 Denmark Street in 1796) and Grace's Guide; confirmed. The merchant stays described.
1822, the apprentice Harvey: Wikipedia and the Science Museum Group (a partner's nephew taken on as apprentice); confirmed.
Bristol Milk: the accounts read call it the old generic Bristol name for sweet sherry, and the firm sold one; the story now says so rather than make it the firm's own name.

Two brothers, 1882, the lady's remark: Wikipedia and Bibendum give the two brothers of the Harvey family and the 1880s; Wikipedia, Atlas Obscura and the house give 1882 for the first sale; the remark in several retellings, told as a legend; confirmed. The house's Spanish sheet says it registered a sherry called Cream in 1880; open.
The Royal Warrant of 1895: the house's heritage page and its Spanish history page (granted under Queen Victoria); confirmed as the house's account, hedged as it is.

The blue bottle: the house says it was the first wine merchant to dress its wines in Bristol blue glass; the story now says, as the house tells it, that it dressed its wines in that glass, and leaves the first out.

More than thirty wines, Fino, Amontillado, Oloroso and Pedro Ximénez; at least three years in American oak: the house's Bristol Cream page and its heritage page (the three years said of all its sherries); confirmed.

Blended in Jerez: the house's questions page says all production and blending has been done in Jerez since the early 1970s, and Wikipedia moves the firm's main premises to Jerez in 1970; the story now dates it.
The serve: the house's 12 degrees Celsius and the Consejo's 10 to 12 for Cream; the story now gives the Consejo's own range.

The others: the house's English page names the VORS Amontillado Fine Old Amontillado and its Spanish sheet Very Old Amontillado, a medium Amontillado certified at thirty years; Harveys Amontillado Medium Dry was in no source read and is cut; the Palo Cortado VORS added from the house's own page.
The questions: four descriptions of a sherry, one right; four Bristol names, the key in every account. Sound.
The rules: nobody living named; no price, no score (the house's competition trophies were read and left out); British; no dash. Sound.
